strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: conventional TTA evaluation ignores the latency cost of adaptation, which matters for real deployment (edge devices, interactive systems, budget-constrained missions).

The three proposed metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are well-motivated by distinct, realistic deployment archetypes and are each accompanied by a clear formal protocol and interpretable decomposition (availability/served-accuracy, responsiveness/accuracy, adapted/frozen accuracy).

Careful, explicit engagement with prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024): the paper identifies concrete limitations (risk-free fallback, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling) and proposes a principled buffered single-model alternative, with a full appendix justifying design choices.

Extensive empirical study: 7 TTA methods × 15 corruptions × 16 temporal scenarios (240 evaluations), with detailed per-corruption and per-scenario decompositions in the appendix that substantiate the main claims (e.g., Tables 3–5, 13–19).

The findings are actionable and non-trivial in their specificity: e.g., quantifying exactly how much accuracy improvement would be needed to overcome availability/responsiveness penalties (computational insolvency), and identifying SHOT-IM's surprising resilience under budget exhaustion due to full-backbone updates.

Good transparency about scope and limitations in the Discussion section (single dataset/architecture, exclusions of certain method classes, episodic i.i.d. assumption), and honest treatment of when methods are mismatched to evaluation context (e.g., LAME).
weaknesses: All experiments use a single architecture (ResNet-50), single dataset/benchmark (ImageNet-C), and single hardware platform (RTX 4080 GPU); despite claims that findings generalize, no evidence is given across different backbones, tasks, or especially embedded/edge hardware, which is central to several of the paper's own motivating examples (drones, wildlife cameras, on-device photo apps).

Results are reported from a single seed with no variance or statistical significance testing (explicitly acknowledged), which weakens confidence in close rank comparisons and the reported Spearman correlations.

The contribution is purely evaluative/diagnostic; no new adaptation method or mitigation strategy is proposed to address the identified failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, unproductive overhead), somewhat limiting the paper's forward-looking impact beyond providing a benchmark lens.

The set of evaluated methods, while reasonable, is relatively dated (Tent 2021, ETA/SAR 2022–2023); the exclusion of more recent multi-forward-pass or wrapper-based methods (justified in the Discussion) limits the currency of the specific empirical conclusions, even though the framework itself would still apply.

Some design choices (hyperbolic decay for continuous utility, specific ρ/T/B grids) are reasonable but not deeply validated against real user studies or system telemetry; the practical translation of these thresholds to arbitrary deployments is left largely to informal analogy (e.g., drone battery, photo app) rather than grounded empirical calibration.

The core high-level finding that gradient-based methods with heavier backward-pass overhead lose out under tight temporal budgets is somewhat expected a priori from known accuracy-cost trade-offs in the TTA literature; the paper's novelty rests more on quantifying and systematizing this than on revealing a wholly unexpected phenomenon.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: TTA methods are almost universally benchmarked assuming unbounded processing time, and this paper systematically operationalizes the accuracy-latency trade-off with three well-motivated utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) tailored to distinct deployment archetypes.

The utility decompositions (availability vs served accuracy, responsiveness vs raw accuracy, adapted vs frozen accuracy) provide genuine mechanistic insight into *why* rankings invert, going beyond a black-box score to explain failure modes such as 'computational insolvency.'

Careful, well-justified improvements over the closest prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024), including a buffered single-model protocol that removes the risk-free fallback assumption, disproportionate ceiling penalties, and forced idling; these design choices are clearly argued and documented (Appendix B).

Extensive empirical coverage for the chosen setting: 7 TTA methods × 15 corruptions × 16 temporal scenarios = 240 evaluations, with thorough per-corruption and per-scenario breakdowns in the appendix.

The central empirical finding—rank instability under temporal pressure, including the offline SOTA method (ETA) losing in ~41% of evaluations—is a clear, actionable, and well-supported result that has real implications for how the TTA literature reports results.
Clear writing, useful notation/terminology tables, and figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 3) that make the rank-instability phenomenon intuitively visible.
weaknesses: Very narrow empirical scope: a single dataset (ImageNet-C), single architecture (ResNet-50), single batch size, and single GPU (RTX 4080). Since latency-derived utility metrics are inherently hardware- and implementation-dependent, it is unclear how much of the reported rank instability is an artifact of this specific measured platform versus a general phenomenon; the paper's own motivating examples (wildlife camera traps, on-device photo tagging, drones) involve very different hardware profiles that are never tested.

Results are reported for a single random seed with no variance/significance analysis across runs; although latency variance is argued to be small, accuracy variance (especially for stochastic/entropy-based methods near collapse thresholds) is not characterized, weakening confidence in fine-grained rank comparisons.

The method pool is limited to 7 fully-TTA methods, explicitly excluding several increasingly prominent categories (multi-forward-pass methods, wrapper-style methods). While the exclusions are justified for tractability, this limits how strongly the 'no clear winner' conclusion generalizes to the current TTA landscape.

The specific parameter grids (HCI thresholds T, utilisation levels ρ, budgets B) are chosen somewhat heuristically (e.g., anchored to Nielsen/Card HCI literature or geometric spacing) without sensitivity analysis showing how robust the qualitative conclusions (e.g., 'rank instability increases with pressure') are to these specific choices.

The paper is purely an evaluation/diagnostic framework; it identifies failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, unproductive overhead) and desiderata (corruption-conditioned allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) but proposes no method or even a minimal baseline addressing them, leaving the practical payoff largely as 'measure your own deployment carefully' rather than a solution.

The hyperbolic decay choice for continuous utility, while grounded in behavioral-economics literature on time discounting, is asserted rather than empirically validated against alternative decay functions (e.g., exponential, linear), and the paper does not discuss how sensitive conclusions are to this functional form.

Evaluation is restricted to the classic episodic, i.i.d. ImageNet-C setting, which the paper itself notes disadvantages methods like LAME designed for non-i.i.d. streams (which loses in all 240 cases); this raises the concern that part of the observed instability reflects evaluation-method mismatch rather than a general temporal-pressure phenomenon, and the more realistic continual/non-stationary settings suggested as future work are not explored despite being central to the paper's real-world motivating scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: conventional TTA evaluation ignores the accuracy-latency trade-off that governs real deployability, and the paper makes a compelling case (with concrete deployment vignettes) for why this matters.

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are each grounded in distinct, well-motivated deployment archetypes (hard-deadline streams, interactive/HCI settings, budget-constrained edge devices) rather than being an arbitrary single metric.

Careful, critical engagement with prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024): the paper identifies three concrete limitations (risk-free fallback evaluation, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling) and proposes a buffered single-model protocol that addresses them, with clear justification in Appendix B.

Extensive empirical scope: 7 methods x 15 corruptions x multiple parameter settings = 240 evaluations, with thorough decomposition tables (availability, responsiveness, adapted/frozen accuracy) that explain *why* rankings invert rather than just reporting that they do.

The utility decompositions surface actionable, non-obvious findings (e.g., SHOT-IM's superior frozen-state stability, the disproportionate cost of backpropagation as 'extrinsic overhead', computational insolvency thresholds) that could genuinely inform future TTA method design.
Clear writing, well-organized figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 3), and thorough appendices with notation tables, method descriptions, and per-corruption breakdowns that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Results are reported for a single random seed (explicitly noted in Appendix C.2/C.3) with no variance estimates or significance testing, despite the paper making fine-grained quantitative claims (e.g., Spearman rs = -0.74 vs 0.21, 41.2% loss rate, 19.3% average utility gap) that would benefit from uncertainty quantification, especially given the central thesis is about rank *instability*.

Evaluation is confined to a single architecture (ResNet-50), single dataset (ImageNet-C), and single hardware platform (RTX 4080); latency-based conclusions (e.g., magnitude of extrinsic overhead, specific insolvency thresholds) are inherently hardware- and implementation-dependent, and the paper's claim in the Discussion that the 'underlying need... remains universal' across modalities/architectures/hardware is asserted rather than empirically supported.

The specific functional forms chosen for the metrics (hyperbolic decay with HCI-motivated threshold T, single-batch buffer size, geometric spacing of parameter sweeps) are reasonable but somewhat heuristic design choices rather than derived from a principled model of user/system utility; sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not examined.

The evaluation remains restricted to the episodic, i.i.d. corruption-shift setting, which the paper itself notes is a mismatch for methods like LAME designed for non-i.i.d. streams (which then trivially underperforms in all 240 cases); this raises the question of how much the reported 'rank instability' is confounded by evaluation-method mismatch versus genuine temporal-pressure effects.

The core methodological contribution builds incrementally on Alfarra et al. (2024)'s discrete formulation, extending it with two additional metrics and a protocol refinement; while valuable, the conceptual novelty is more in scope/systematization than in fundamentally new technique.
No code/artifact availability statement is visible in the excerpted text beyond a mention of a 'supplementary code repository', making full reproducibility hard to verify from the manuscript alone.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in TTA evaluation: the accuracy-latency trade-off is typically ignored in offline benchmarking despite being critical for real deployments.

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are well-motivated, grounded in physical units (ms) rather than model-relative proxies, and each is accompanied by a clear decomposition (availability, responsiveness, adapt/frozen accuracy) that provides interpretable diagnosis of failure modes rather than just aggregate numbers.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 750+ temporal evaluations across 11 TTA methods, multiple architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), multiple datasets (ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10-C), and multiple hardware platforms (RTX 4080 GPU, Raspberry Pi 5 CPU), demonstrating that the central finding (rank instability) generalizes broadly.

Careful, well-justified revision of prior work's (Alfarra et al.) discrete evaluation protocol, addressing concrete flaws (risk-free fallback, disproportionate penalties, forced idling) with a principled buffered single-model design, and transparent side-by-side comparison in the appendix.

The failure-mode analysis (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, harmful adaptation) leads to concrete, well-argued design principles (corruption-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) that give actionable guidance for future TTA method design.

Strong attention to reproducibility and transparency: detailed appendices document implementation choices (e.g., batch-norm running-buffer handling), timing methodology, and provide per-batch decomposition tables; code is promised for release.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (single seed, exclusion of certain method classes, episodic i.i.d. assumption) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: All main experiments are run with a single seed; while the authors claim seed variance is negligible (citing prior work), no direct variance/error bars are reported for Tempora's own metrics, which is a concern given some utility gaps between methods are small (e.g., a few percentage points in Table 23).

The evaluation remains restricted to episodic, i.i.d. batch sampling, which is acknowledged as a mismatch for continual/non-stationary methods (e.g., LAME's uniform failure), potentially limiting how far conclusions transfer to more realistic streaming conditions; this is left entirely to future work rather than even a preliminary exploration.

Design choices within each utility metric (hyperbolic discounting form for continuous utility, single-batch buffer size for discrete, fixed batch size of 64) are motivated qualitatively but not stress-tested with sensitivity analyses, so it is unclear how robust the reported rank instability is to these modeling choices.

The headline qualitative finding—that offline rankings do not predict rankings under latency pressure, and that slower/more sophisticated gradient-based methods lose out—is intuitive given the construction of the metrics (overhead directly penalizes availability/responsiveness); the paper's main novelty lies more in the systematic measurement framework than in a surprising empirical discovery, which somewhat limits the significance of the core result relative to the depth of engineering effort.

Method coverage, while reasonable, excludes several relevant TTA variants (DDA, MEMO, wrapper-style methods) that the authors themselves note could interact interestingly with temporal constraints, and this exclusion is justified more by tractability than principled scoping.

Hardware diversity for the main results is limited to one GPU; the CPU-based experiments use only a single low-power edge device (Raspberry Pi) with a different backbone/dataset (ResNet-18/CIFAR-10-C) rather than being integrated into the main ImageNet-C/ResNet-50 or ViT-B/16 analysis, making cross-hardware comparisons somewhat fragmented across separate mini-studies.

strengths: Clear and important motivation: aggregate offline accuracy benchmarks for TTA genuinely ignore the latency cost that determines real-world viability, and the paper articulates this gap, and its relation to prior work (Alfarra et al. 2024, Ghunaim et al. 2023), carefully.

The three utility archetypes (discrete, continuous, amortised) are sensible formalizations covering distinct deployment regimes (hard deadlines, interactive decay, budget-constrained), and each is accompanied by a decomposition (availability, responsiveness, adapt/frozen split) that offers genuine diagnostic value beyond a single scalar metric.

Very extensive empirical scope: 9-11 TTA methods, multiple architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), multiple datasets (ImageNet-C/R/V2, CIFAR-10-C), and multiple hardware platforms (GPU, Raspberry Pi CPU), with 750+ temporal evaluations and detailed per-corruption breakdowns in the appendix.

Thoughtful, well-argued revision of the discrete evaluation protocol from Alfarra et al., identifying and fixing concrete flaws (risk-free fallback models, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling) with a buffered single-model simulation; the ablation in Table 8 convincingly shows this changes conclusions (e.g., AdaBN's rank).
Good transparency around implementation subtleties (e.g., BN running-statistics handling under frozen inference) and an honest limitations section acknowledging exclusions and the single-seed caveat.
weaknesses: All headline results are computed from a single seed (2025) with no repeated runs or confidence intervals for accuracy, timing, or the derived utility rankings; this is a significant soundness concern for a paper whose central claims ("rank instability," Spearman correlations across 240+ cells) are precisely about small, potentially noise-sensitive differences between method rankings. The claim that seed variance is 'negligible' is asserted by citing Alfarra et al. rather than demonstrated for this paper's own setup, metrics, and hardware.

The core empirical finding — that latency-unaware rankings fail to predict latency-constrained rankings, and that simple/fast methods win under tight budgets — is intuitively expected given how the discrete/continuous/amortised metrics are constructed (methods with near-zero overhead such as NEO/AdaBN trivially achieve near-100% availability/responsiveness). The paper documents this thoroughly but offers comparatively modest new conceptual insight beyond confirming and extending Alfarra et al.'s qualitative conclusion with a broader, better-grounded set of scenarios.

The three 'necessary properties' for deployable adaptation (corruption-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) are asserted as design targets but never operationalized, tested, or shown achievable; no new method or even a toy fix is proposed to validate that these properties are sufficient or practically attainable, leaving this contribution largely rhetorical.

Several key design choices remain under-justified or arbitrary: the 6σ provision for λ, the specific geometric spacing of ρ/T/B sweep values, and the particular HCI thresholds, all of which materially affect which method 'wins' in a given cell; sensitivity of the main conclusions to these choices is not analyzed.

The paper is purely an evaluation/benchmarking contribution restricted to episodic image-classification corruption benchmarks; claims of generality to other modalities, tasks, and non-i.i.d./continual streams are stated as future work and discussion rather than demonstrated, which somewhat overstates the 'universal' framing in the abstract/discussion.

The manuscript is extremely dense with appendix tables (dozens of pages) that, while thorough, risk being data dumps rather than synthesized evidence; the main text's headline statistics (e.g., '211/240 cases', '15% average utility yielded') are somewhat cherry-picked summary numbers whose robustness is hard to assess without variance information.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in TTA evaluation: the accuracy-latency trade-off under realistic deployment constraints, which is a timely and practically important contribution as TTA methods grow more complex.

The three-archetype taxonomy (discrete/environment-led, continuous/user-led, amortised/resource-led) is well-motivated with concrete deployment examples and grounded in physical units (ms) rather than model-relative proxies used by prior work (Alfarra et al.), which substantially improves interpretability and cross-model/cross-hardware comparability.

Careful, principled critique and revision of the closest prior work's discrete protocol (risk-free fallback evaluation, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling), with clear justification and empirical demonstration (Table 8/9) of the impact of these design choices.

Utility decomposition into interpretable sub-terms (availability, responsiveness, adapted/frozen accuracy) enables diagnosis of *why* rankings change, not just *whether* they do, and surfaces three distinct, well-articulated failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, harmful adaptation).

Extremely extensive empirical validation: 750+ (and in the appendix, 1000+) evaluations across 11 TTA methods, multiple architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), datasets (ImageNet-C/R/V2, CIFAR-10-C), and hardware platforms (RTX 4080 GPU, Raspberry Pi 5 CPU), consistently reproducing the central rank-instability finding.

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed method descriptions, implementation notes (e.g., BN running-statistics handling), full notation/terminology tables, and per-corruption/per-scenario result tables in the appendix.
Honest and specific limitations section (method coverage, i.i.d./episodic scope, single-seed, hyperparameter defaults) that does not overstate generality.
weaknesses: Results are reported on a single seed throughout; while the authors note this matches prior practice and claim negligible seed variance, no quantitative evidence (e.g., error bars, multi-seed re-runs) is provided in this submission to support that claim for the new metrics introduced here.

All methods use default hyperparameters only; given that the paper's central claim is about rank instability, it remains unclear how sensitive these rankings are to hyperparameter tuning, especially for gradient-based methods with reliability/redundancy filtering thresholds that directly interact with the timing-driven failure modes being measured.

Several core design choices in the metrics (e.g., hyperbolic discount form and its argument scaling, single-batch buffer size, the specific grid of ρ/T/B values) are reasonable but not rigorously justified or stress-tested for sensitivity; alternative decay functions or buffer policies could plausibly shift conclusions.

The evaluation remains confined to classification under covariate shift (corruption benchmarks); non-i.i.d./non-stationary streams and other modalities/tasks are explicitly left to future work, which somewhat limits the generality of the claimed 'universal' design properties despite the broad sweep over architectures and hardware.

The paper is primarily a benchmarking/evaluation-methodology contribution rather than a new algorithm; its long-term significance depends on community adoption, and the extremely dense appendix (35+ pages of tables) suggests the core paper alone may not be fully self-contained for assessing the robustness of the central claims.

Framing the contribution as enabling 'the first' systematic evaluation across temporal constraints is somewhat strong given Alfarra et al. already established the discrete temporal-pressure paradigm; the paper's novelty is more incremental (broader taxonomy, physical-unit grounding, decomposition) than foundational, though it is still a meaningful advance.
